lessons.title: Middleware & CORS
lessons.html:
Custom Middleware and Cross-Origin Requests

Middleware processes requests globally before they reach route handlers. CORS is essential for web apps calling your API from different domains.

Custom Timing Middleware:

from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
from starlette.middleware.base import BaseHTTPMiddleware
import time

class TimingMiddleware(BaseHTTPMiddleware):
    async def dispatch(self, request: Request, call_next):
        start = time.perf_counter()
        response = await call_next(request)
        process_time = time.perf_counter() - start
        response.headers["X-Process-Time"] = str(process_time)
        return response

app = FastAPI()
app.add_middleware(TimingMiddleware)

CORS Configuration:

from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware

origins = ["http://localhost:3000", "https://myapp.example.com"]

app.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=origins,
    allow_credentials=True,
    allow_methods=["GET", "POST", "PUT", "DELETE", "PATCH"],
    allow_headers=["*"],
    expose_headers=["X-Request-ID", "X-Process-Time"],
    max_age=600,
)

Practice Exercises:

  1. Create a middleware that logs all requests to a database
  2. Implement rate limiting middleware using token bucket
  3. Add request ID propagation middleware for tracing

Key Takeaways:

  • Middleware wraps all route handlers
  • CORS must be configured for browser-based clients
  • Middleware order matters for request processing

lessons.title: File Uploads & Streaming
lessons.html:
Handling File Uploads and Streaming Responses

FastAPI handles file uploads with UploadFile. Streaming responses serve large files without loading them into memory.

File Upload:

from fastapi import FastAPI, UploadFile, File
import shutil
from pathlib import Path

app = FastAPI()
UPLOAD_DIR = Path("./uploads")
UPLOAD_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

@app.post("/files/upload/")
async def upload_file(file: UploadFile = File(...)):
    file_path = UPLOAD_DIR / file.filename
    with file_path.open("wb") as buffer:
        shutil.copyfileobj(file.file, buffer)
    return {"filename": file.filename, "size": file_path.stat().st_size}

Streaming CSV:

from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
import csv, io

@app.get("/export/users/csv/")
async def export_users_csv():
    def generate():
        output = io.StringIO()
        writer = csv.writer(output)
        writer.writerow(["ID", "Name", "Email"])
        for i in range(10000):
            writer.writerow([i, f"User {i}", f"user{i}@ex.com"])
            yield output.getvalue()
            output.seek(0)
            output.truncate(0)
    return StreamingResponse(generate(), media_type="text/csv",
        headers={"Content-Disposition": "attachment; filename=users.csv"})

Practice Exercises:

  1. Build an image upload endpoint with thumbnail generation
  2. Stream video files with range request support
  3. Implement multipart upload for large files

Key Takeaways:

  • UploadFile streams files without loading entirely in memory
  • StreamingResponse is ideal for large datasets
  • Generator functions yield data lazily

lessons.title: WebSockets with FastAPI
lessons.html:
Real-Time Communication with WebSockets

WebSockets enable bidirectional, real-time communication between clients and servers.

Connection Manager:

from fastapi import FastAPI, WebSocket, WebSocketDisconnect
from typing import Set

app = FastAPI()

class ConnectionManager:
    def __init__(self):
        self.active: Set[WebSocket] = set()

    async def connect(self, ws: WebSocket):
        await ws.accept()
        self.active.add(ws)

    def disconnect(self, ws: WebSocket):
        self.active.remove(ws)

    async def broadcast(self, message: str):
        for conn in self.active:
            await conn.send_text(message)

manager = ConnectionManager()

WebSocket Endpoint:

@app.websocket("/ws/{client_id}")
async def websocket_endpoint(ws: WebSocket, client_id: str):
    await manager.connect(ws)
    try:
        await manager.broadcast(f"Client {client_id} joined")
        while True:
            data = await ws.receive_text()
            await manager.broadcast(f"{client_id}: {data}")
    except WebSocketDisconnect:
        manager.disconnect(ws)
        await manager.broadcast(f"{client_id} left")

Practice Exercises:

  1. Build a real-time chat application with rooms
  2. Implement a live notification system
  3. Add WebSocket authentication middleware

Key Takeaways:

  • WebSockets provide full-duplex communication
  • Connection manager tracks active clients
  • WebSocketDisconnect signals client departure

lessons.title: Rate Limiting & Security Headers
lessons.html:
API Protection and Security

Rate limiting prevents abuse. Security headers protect against common web vulnerabilities.

Rate Limiting:

from slowapi import Limiter, _rate_limit_exceeded_handler
from slowapi.util import get_remote_address
from slowapi.errors import RateLimitExceeded

limiter = Limiter(key_func=get_remote_address)
app = FastAPI()
app.state.limiter = limiter
app.add_exception_handler(RateLimitExceeded, _rate_limit_exceeded_handler)

@app.get("/api/public/")
@limiter.limit("10/minute")
async def public_endpoint():
    return {"message": "rate limited"}

Security Headers:

class SecurityHeadersMiddleware(BaseHTTPMiddleware):
    async def dispatch(self, request, call_next):
        response = await call_next(request)
        response.headers["X-Content-Type-Options"] = "nosniff"
        response.headers["X-Frame-Options"] = "DENY"
        response.headers["Strict-Transport-Security"] = "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains"
        response.headers["Content-Security-Policy"] = "default-src 'self'"
        response.headers["Permissions-Policy"] = "camera=(), microphone=()"
        return response

Practice Exercises:

  1. Set up tiered rate limiting (free/paid tiers)
  2. Implement API key authentication with rate limiting per key
  3. Scan headers for security vulnerabilities

Key Takeaways:

  • Rate limiting protects against DDoS and abuse
  • Security headers mitigate XSS, clickjacking, and MIME sniffing
  • HTTPS + security headers = defense in depth

GraphQL API with Python

lessons.title: Celery Task Queue
lessons.html:
Background Task Processing with Celery

Celery is the most popular distributed task queue for Python. Handles email, image processing, and report generation.

Celery Setup:

from celery import Celery

celery_app = Celery(
    "tasks",
    broker="redis://localhost:6379/0",
    backend="redis://localhost:6379/0"
)

celery_app.conf.update(
    task_serializer="json",
    result_serializer="json",
    timezone="UTC",
    task_track_started=True,
    task_acks_late=True,
)

@celery_app.task(bind=True, max_retries=3, default_retry_delay=60)
def send_email_task(self, to_email, subject, body):
    try:
        # send email
        return {"status": "sent", "to": to_email}
    except Exception as exc:
        raise self.retry(exc=exc)

FastAPI Integration:

@app.post("/send-email/")
async def send_email(request: EmailRequest):
    task = send_email_task.delay(request.to, request.subject, request.body)
    return {"message": "Queued", "task_id": task.id}

@app.get("/tasks/{task_id}/")
async def get_task_status(task_id: str):
    task = send_email_task.AsyncResult(task_id)
    if task.failed():
        return {"status": "failed", "error": str(task.info)}
    return {"status": task.state}

Practice Exercises:

  1. Create a task that generates PDF reports
  2. Implement task chaining for multi-step workflows
  3. Monitor Celery workers with Flower dashboard

Key Takeaways:

  • Tasks run asynchronously outside the request cycle
  • Retries with backoff handle transient failures
  • Task IDs allow status polling from clients

lessons.title: API Caching with Redis
lessons.html:
Redis Caching Strategies for APIs

Caching reduces database load and improves response times significantly.

Cache Decorator:

import redis, json, hashlib
from functools import wraps

redis_client = redis.Redis(host="localhost", port=6379, db=0, decode_responses=True)

def cache(ttl_seconds=300):
    def decorator(func):
        @wraps(func)
        async def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
            key_parts = [func.__name__] + [str(a) for a in args]
            cache_key = hashlib.md5("|".join(key_parts).encode()).hexdigest()
            cached = redis_client.get(cache_key)
            if cached:
                return json.loads(cached)
            result = await func(*args, **kwargs)
            redis_client.setex(cache_key, ttl_seconds, json.dumps(result))
            return result
        return wrapper
    return decorator

@app.get("/api/popular/")
@cache(ttl_seconds=60)
async def get_popular():
    return db.query(User).order_by(User.followers.desc()).limit(10).all()

Cache Invalidation:

class CacheManager:
    def invalidate_pattern(self, pattern: str):
        cursor = 0
        while True:
            cursor, keys = self.redis.scan(cursor, match=pattern, count=100)
            if keys:
                self.redis.delete(*keys)
            if cursor == 0:
                break

    async def after_user_update(self, user_id):
        self.invalidate_pattern(f"get_user*{user_id}*")
        self.invalidate_pattern("get_popular*")

Practice Exercises:

  1. Implement write-through vs write-behind caching
  2. Add distributed caching with Redis Cluster
  3. Monitor cache hit rate and optimize TTLs

Key Takeaways:

  • Caching improves API response times by 10-100x
  • Cache invalidation is the hardest part of caching
  • Redis supports complex data structures beyond simple key-value

lessons.title: API Versioning Strategies
lessons.html:
Smooth API Versioning

API versioning lets you evolve your API without breaking existing clients.

URL Path Versioning:

from fastapi import APIRouter

v1 = APIRouter(prefix="/api/v1", tags=["v1"])
v2 = APIRouter(prefix="/api/v2", tags=["v2"])

@v1.get("/users/")
async def get_users_v1():
    return [{"id": 1, "name": "Alice", "email": "alice@ex.com"}]

@v2.get("/users/")
async def get_users_v2(page: int = 1, per_page: int = 20):
    users = get_users_paginated(page, per_page)
    return {"data": users, "pagination": {"page": page, "per_page": per_page,
        "total": count_users()}}

app.include_router(v1)
app.include_router(v2)

Header Versioning:

@app.get("/api/users/")
async def get_users(request: Request):
    version = request.headers.get("Accept-Version", "2025-01-01")
    handlers = {"2023-01-01": handle_v1, "2025-01-01": handle_v2}
    if version not in handlers:
        raise HTTPException(400, f"Unsupported version: {version}")
    return await handlers[version](request)

Practice Exercises:

  1. Design versioned API for a social media platform
  2. Implement sunset headers for deprecated versions
  3. Create migration guides for breaking changes

Key Takeaways:

  • URL versioning is simplest but leads to URL duplication
  • Header versioning keeps URLs clean
  • Always document deprecated features with sunset dates

lessons.title: Production Monitoring & Health Checks
lessons.html:
API Health Checks and Structured Logging

Production APIs need health checks, monitoring, and structured logging for reliability.

Health Check:

from pydantic import BaseModel
import psutil, time
from datetime import datetime

class HealthStatus(BaseModel):
    status: str
    version: str
    timestamp: str
    database: str
    redis: str
    memory_usage: float
    cpu_percent: float

app = FastAPI()
start_time = time.time()

@app.get("/health/", response_model=HealthStatus)
async def health():
    db_status = "healthy" if check_db() else "unhealthy"
    redis_status = "healthy" if check_redis() else "unhealthy"
    return HealthStatus(
        status="ok" if db_status == "healthy" else "degraded",
        version="2.0.0",
        timestamp=datetime.utcnow().isoformat(),
        uptime_seconds=time.time() - start_time,
        database=db_status,
        redis=redis_status,
        memory_usage=psutil.virtual_memory().percent,
        cpu_percent=psutil.cpu_percent(interval=1),
    )

Structured Logging:

from loguru import logger
import sys

logger.configure(handlers=[
    {"sink": sys.stdout, "serialize": True},
    {"sink": "logs/api.log", "rotation": "500 MB", "retention": "30 days", "serialize": True},
])

@app.middleware("http")
async def log_requests(request, call_next):
    start = time.time()
    response = await call_next(request)
    logger.info("API Request", extra={
        "method": request.method, "path": request.url.path,
        "status": response.status_code,
        "duration_ms": round((time.time() - start) * 1000, 2),
        "client_ip": request.client.host,
    })
    return response

Practice Exercises:

  1. Set up Grafana dashboards for API metrics
  2. Implement alerting for error rate spikes
  3. Add structured logging with correlation IDs

Key Takeaways:

  • Health checks enable automated recovery
  • Structured JSON logs are machine-parseable
  • Monitoring metrics guide capacity planning
